S27-001 · BossFang Strategy — The Governed Claw and the Universal Harness

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

BossFang Strategy — The Governed Claw and the Universal Harness

Scope: BossFang/librefang's expanded role: an always-on personal-assistant gateway ("claw"-class functionality) and the container that unifies agent execution across UAR, external AI harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, …), and workflow orchestration — under one identity, governance, and audit plane.

Status: v1.0 strategy, 2026-07-18. Builds on docs/strategies/agents/README.md (placements; sidecar = minimal local BossFang), docs/strategies/plugins/README.md (capabilities, governance/identity §9, settings substrate §11), docs/strategies/skill-support/README.md (outbound MCP), and the flint stack (FRF bridges/media, flint-gate, Flint Vault).

S27-002 · 1. What BossFang already is, and what it becomes

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

1. What BossFang already is, and what it becomes

Today (FUNC-SPEC §07 + FRF/forge reality): OFP sync peer · remote model server · UAR agent container · the deployment target for always-on Hands. This document adds two roles that complete it:

  1. Channel gateway — messaging/voice ingress (the "claw" role): the assistant is reachable from WhatsApp/Telegram/Matrix/etc. and works while every screen is off.
  2. Harness orchestrator — external agent runtimes (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, …) execute inside BossFang's governance envelope, unified with native UAR agents.

Both arrive as capability plugins (knowme:channel, knowme:harness) — no new subsystem kinds, the §1-inversion of the plugins doc doing its job.

S27-003 · 1.1 The vendored base (2026-07-18)

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

1.1 The vendored base (2026-07-18)

The GQAdonis/librefang fork (BossFang — "Libre Agent Operating System", community fork of openfang; 24 crates, 2,100+ tests) is vendored as a submodule at rust/vendor/librefang. It is not a blank canvas — large parts of this document already exist there and this strategy becomes a customization and integration plan rather than a build plan:

Strategy concern librefang crate(s) already providing it
Channel gateway (§3) librefang-channels — "pluggable messaging integrations"
Hands (§1, agents doc) librefang-hands — "curated autonomous capability packages"
Skills + marketplace + claw compat (skill-support doc) librefang-skills — "registry, loader, marketplace, and OpenClaw compatibility"
UAR agent metadata librefang-uar-spec — UAR-AGENT-MD parser + AgentManifest translator
Harness/IDE embedding librefang-acp — Agent Client Protocol adapter (Zed/VSCode/JetBrains over stdio JSON-RPC); librefang-subprocess + librefang-runtime-sandbox-docker for driving external CLIs sandboxed
Extensions + credentials librefang-extensions — one-click MCP setup, credential vault, OAuth2 PKCE
Memory/karpathy wiki librefang-memory, librefang-memory-wiki — durable markdown vault with provenance frontmatter
Governance/audit hooks librefang-runtime-audit, librefang-kernel-metering, librefang-kernel-router
Model drivers librefang-llm-driver(s)

Integration posture: KnowMe-specific behavior (Cedar dual-identity per plugins doc §9, OFP profile, the capability-card vocabulary, settings substrate) lands as adapters and upstreamable patches around these crates, keeping the submodule tracking its upstream; the ACP adapter also opens a fourth harness direction — BossFang agents embedded into Zed/VSCode/JetBrains, not just external harnesses embedded into BossFang. The gap analysis between librefang-skills' OpenClaw-compat model and this stack's structural-boundary claims (§2) is the first integration task.

Alongside librefang, the Universal Agent Runtime is vendored at rust/vendor/universal-agent-runtime (v1.0.0): it is the "UAR agent container" in this doc's role list — served as the server-full bundle on peers, as the uar-sidecar binary on desktop, and linked embedded on mobile (see docs/strategies/agents/README.md §7 for the placement mapping). BossFang's job is serving and governing that container, not reimplementing it.

S27-004 · 2. Positioning: the claw with a real boundary

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

Explicit amendments:
  • Key control does not establish reverse-DNS namespace ownership; separate registry proof is required.

2. Positioning: the claw with a real boundary

The claw category (OpenClaw) proved enormous demand for an always-on personal agent gateway. Its own security documentation states the limits of its model: "not a hostile multi-tenant security boundary"; one trusted operator per gateway; if multiple people can message the bot "they share its delegated tool authority"; prompt injection "not solved by system prompt guardrails alone"; plugins run in-process as trusted code. Mitigations are configuration hygiene (allowlists, tokens, file permissions, a security audit command).

BossFang's claim is categorical, not incremental: the properties OpenClaw documents as out of scope are the properties this stack already enforces structurally.

Threat (OpenClaw's own list) Their mitigation BossFang's structure
Prompt injection from channels Model choice + guardrails Cedar at the tool gate — an injected instruction cannot exceed the agent's policy regardless of what the model believes (FUNC-SPEC §06)
Shared delegated authority DM pairing/allowlist config Untrusted principals (§3.2): senders are identities with scoped grants, not co-owners of the bot's tools
Tool blast radius Deny-lists, sandbox flags Per-agent, per-skill grants; budgets in governance blocks; deny-by-default
Plugin supply chain "Treat plugin folders as trusted code" WASM sandbox + reviewed capability/permission cards + signatures
Exposed gateway Loopback + token hygiene flint-gate auth, mTLS peers, did:key: payload encryption (OFP)
"What did it do?" Log review Hash-chained audit keyed on (user, agent, capability, action)

We adopt their genuinely good UX-level inventions as schema'd defaults (§3.3) and their security audit idea as a first-class posture tool (§6). We do not adopt their trust model.

S27-005 · 3. The channel gateway (`knowme:channel`)

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

3. The channel gateway (knowme:channel)

S27-006 · 3.1 Transport is already built

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

3.1 Transport is already built

FRF ships Matrix inbound (live /sync streaming), ATProto outbound (writes to a PDS), and media via LiveKit + str0m (negotiation proven) — channels are adapters over existing bridge machinery, not new infrastructure. Each channel is a capability plugin: settings schema (account/pairing config; secrets → Vault), events (message-received, delivery-status), actions (send, react), and chunk support for streaming replies into chat-shaped channels.

S27-007 · 3.2 Ingress principals — the structural upgrade

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

3.2 Ingress principals — the structural upgrade

Every external sender resolves to a principal: paired senders map to known contacts (with explicit, scoped grants: "may converse", "may trigger the Reading-List Hand", never blanket); unknown senders are untrusted by construction. Cedar context on every action carries channel, sender, and trust-tier, so policy can say things config files can't: "content originating from channel senders may never parameterize shell-exec for any agent". Channel content enters the pipeline tagged (provenance discipline from agents doc §3) — it can trigger, it cannot authorize.

S27-008 · 3.3 Adopted UX patterns (as settings schemas, defaults conservative)

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

3.3 Adopted UX patterns (as settings schemas, defaults conservative)

Pairing-code first contact; allowlist mode; group mention-gating; per-sender session isolation (each channel+sender pair is its own conversation context); reply-context visibility limits. All are fields on the channel capability's settings schema — auditable, syncable, org-overridable — not hand-edited config.

S27-009 · 3.4 Reach

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

3.4 Reach

Where the user is: DM the assistant from the phone's messenger when the KnowMe app isn't installed (or is out of reach); voice in/out via the media plane later. Every conversation ingested through a channel is a normal KnowMe conversation — synced, searchable, memory-connected — because it lands in the same entity graph.

S27-010 · 4. The harness orchestrator (`knowme:harness`)

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

4. The harness orchestrator (knowme:harness)

S27-011 · 4.1 The unification claim

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

4.1 The unification claim

Codex Desktop orchestrates OpenAI's runtime; Claude's apps orchestrate Claude. KnowMe + BossFang orchestrates all of them, plus local models, under one plane: one identity model (each harness task runs under an agent DID; RFC 8693 act claims), one governance model (Cedar wraps every harness's tool activity at the boundary), one audit trail, one model-routing layer (liter-llm + local engines), one UI (Hands, conversations, A2UI). The prometheus-skill-pack already targets ten-plus harnesses for authoring; this is the identical neutrality applied to execution.

S27-012 · 4.2 The adapter contract

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

4.2 The adapter contract

A harness adapter is a capability plugin declaring knowme:harness:

  • Execution: spawns the harness CLI in a sandbox (container/jail; workspace mounts declared and reviewed like any permission; no host-direct default);
  • Translation: harness I/O ⇄ AgentService/A2A tasks with frf-agentproto ContentBlocks — which is precisely the crate's design center; streaming progress becomes ordinary chunk traffic (A2UI-renderable);
  • Credentials: harness API keys live in Flint Vault / keychain, injected into the sandbox at spawn, never stored in workspaces (the classic harness foot-gun);
  • Settings schema: per-harness model prefs, workspace roots, tool allowances, concurrency caps;
  • Metering: tokens/cost per harness run feed the same local usage stats that drive suggestions (model-config doc §7) — "this workflow ran 3× cheaper via local Qwen3-Coder than via harness X" is a card we can actually show.

A Hand's Step 2 can therefore select executor = UAR (native), a WASM component agent, or a harness adapter — Step 3's placement unchanged. Same wizard, same audit, same pause/resume.

S27-013 · 4.3 Workflow orchestration

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

4.3 Workflow orchestration

BossFang's workflow layer composes across executors: A2A tasks between native Hands, agent-exposed skills (skill-support doc §2), and harness tasks — fan-out, gates, sequencing — with the kbd-orchestrator waypoint pattern (phased plans, assessments, sign-offs) as the proven shape for long multi-phase work. Workflows are themselves declarative artifacts: shareable, governable, auditable like everything else.

S27-014 · 4.4 Honest constraints

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

4.4 Honest constraints

Vendor CLIs change and their ToS govern automation — adapters pin versions and stay within each vendor's supported headless modes; a harness is only as controllable as its flags allow (some tool-permission surfaces are coarse; Cedar then gates at the sandbox boundary: filesystem scope, network egress, secret access); harness runs are the one place where prompt-level governance is advisory — which is exactly why the sandbox + Vault + audit boundary is the enforcement line.

S27-015 · 5. Placement continuity

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

5. Placement continuity

The agents-doc placement table needs no change: sidecar = minimal local BossFang. Claw features are configuration on any placement — a laptop sidecar can run channels while the lid is open; the M4-mini "always-on Hands node" (local-models doc §10) is the natural home; a VPS personal-cloud instance serves the road. One contract, and Settings → Instances already renders the topology. Channels default off on non-always-on placements to avoid the "assistant that answers only when my laptop is awake" trap — the wizard says which instance will answer.

S27-016 · 6. Posture audit (adopt the idea, exceed the implementation)

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

6. Posture audit (adopt the idea, exceed the implementation)

bossfang audit (forge-cli verb + Settings surface): walks channel policies × granted tools × agent policies and reports reachable authority — "an unknown Telegram sender can reach: nothing. A paired sender can reach: conversation + Reading-List trigger." Because grants, principals, and policies are data (not config-file convention), the audit is a query with proofs, not a lint. Ship it in the same release as the first channel plugin; it is the trust story's demo.

S27-017 · 7. Open questions

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

7. Open questions

  1. Channel plugin placement — channels only on sidecar/peer placements (default), or allow phone-local channel bridges (iMessage requires a Mac anyway)?
  2. Sender identity portability — pairing a sender on one instance: does the grant sync across the user's mesh (user-scoped) or stay per-instance (device-scoped)? Default: user-scoped identity, per-instance reachability.
  3. Harness sandbox tier on macOS — containers vs. dedicated OS user vs. seatbelt profiles; pick per-OS defaults and document the guarantees honestly.
  4. Voice loop scope — str0m negotiation is proven but full sovereign SFU is deferred in FRF; sequence voice channels after text channels ship.
  5. Naming — "BossFang" (product) vs "librefang" (OSS core) boundary for the channel/harness features: which land in the open core?

S27-018 · 8. Implementation map

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

8. Implementation map

  • FRF: channel adapters over frf-bridge-matrix/frf-bridge-atproto patterns; a generic channel-adapter trait in frf-librefang (bus + tenant-actor registry already exist); sender-principal mapping into the identity plane.
  • flint-gate: actor-token issuance for harness runs; pairing-code flows.
  • knowme_plugin_host: knowme:channel + knowme:harness cards in the recognized registry (plugins doc §3 table grows by two).
  • Adapters (first wave): Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode — one shared sandbox/translation core, thin per-harness shims.
  • KnowMe app: Instances panel shows channel/harness capabilities per instance; Hands wizard executor selection; audit views for channel-originated runs.
  • bossfang audit in forge-cli; posture panel in Settings → Privacy.

S27-019 · 9. References

Governing revision: IM-01–04 · source requirement, not release evidence.

9. References

  • OpenClaw · security model · docs · assistant setup · freeCodeCamp: build & secure a personal agent with OpenClaw
  • In-repo: docs/strategies/agents/README.md · docs/strategies/plugins/README.md · docs/strategies/skill-support/README.md · FRF README.md (phase 18: Matrix inbound, ATProto outbound, str0m negotiation) · frf-agentproto, frf-librefang

title: Acceptance gates and measurable failure cases
text:
| Gate | Required scenario and pass condition |
|---|---|
| G01 Source coverage | Every inventoried technical section/requirement has a stable source hash, retained detail location, owning revised clause and disposition; zero unexplained omissions. |
| G02 Home continuity | Empty, populated, stale, offline, denied and failed dashboards at compact/tablet/desktop widths; suggestions never execute without submission; restore draft/card state after restart. |
| G03 Container isolation | Cross-user/tenant/project read and mutation attempts fail at the service boundary; badge counts and semantic search do not leak hidden containers. |
| G04 Intent reconciliation | Duplicate submission, lost reply, process kill, conflict, revocation and scope change preserve identities and never replay an old command under new authority. |
| G05 Plugin admission | Tampered hash, invalid signature, namespace squatting, undeclared import, new privilege, missing profile and malicious archive all fail safely. |
| G06 Runtime limits | Infinite compute, memory growth, slow host I/O, recursion and flood events hit distinct enforced limits; a failed plugin cannot wedge the UI or leave an unbounded queue. |
| G07 A2UI parity | Shared fixtures on React and Flutter in light/dark, compact/wide and large text; unknown components inert; local echo and semantic actions preserve schema/version identity. |
| G08 FFI lifecycle | Repeated boot, stream disposal, cancelled run, panic/error propagation and background/foreground transitions do not duplicate engines, leak subscriptions or block the UI. |
| G09 Personal dot | Local default, explicit conversation cloud route, separated memory, editable/exportable beliefs, five honest commitment outcomes, no unsolicited third-party contact. |
| G10 Project coach | Stale evidence, exhausted allowance, scope creep, denied task, healthy silence and restart cases satisfy every PD requirement; KBD remains verdict owner. |
| G11 Human media | One-to-one and multiparty audio/video, permission denial, headset switch, reconnect, late join, participant removal and end-room tested with distinct accounts/devices. |
| G12 Agent media | One-to-one and multiparty room arbitration, overlapping speech, barge-in, echoed audio, worker crash, revoked dot grant and repeated tool request; no duplicate effect or private-memory leak. |
| G13 Data consent | Recording/transcription/agent processing independently consented; decline remains usable; encrypted mode compatibility and plaintext endpoints disclosed accurately. |
| G14 Context | Exact budget invariant, paired tool messages, retrieval provenance, summarizer degradation, thermal limits and cloud-refusal behavior measured on real model artifacts. |
| G15 Accessibility | Keyboard-only controls, screen-reader labels, focus return, contrast, reduced motion, dynamic type and no page-level horizontal overflow. |
| G16 Publication | Hash final files, verify public HTML and every required asset, render desktop/mobile, inspect diagrams, keep receipt with actual CID and observed URLs. |

Performance values are proposed targets pending measurements: local navigation should respond within one frame budget where possible; permission/action validation and first useful feedback should be bounded and visibly pending; media tests must record join time, RTT, packet loss, jitter, first response, interruption latency, CPU, memory, battery and thermal state. Do not turn an unmeasured target into a marketing number.

Release evidence records build/commit digest, host/runtime/catalog versions, device/OS, test inputs, timestamp, result and known gaps. A desktop screenshot cannot certify an iOS plugin runtime. A room with two tracks cannot certify multiparty agent turn-taking. A source file named `sandbox` cannot certify a secure installer.


### Detailed acceptance families

Home tests assert honest freshness and failure states; permission-safe counts; one focused composer; draft-preserving failed sends; suggestions that only prepare drafts; stable focus during refresh; restore behavior; and all 22 screen states. Workspace tests assert context switching, artifact revision identity, canvas navigation without unintended cancellation, legacy prefill without saving, and layout persistence.

A2UI tests cover protocol/catalog negotiation; ordered updates; unresolved-child handling; unknown components; schema-invalid actions; host-owned approvals; malicious text/URLs; explicit action context; dirty-field conflicts; snapshot recovery; native/web parity; and disabled/revoked-plugin recovery. Run tests cover interrupt completion and continuation, multiple outstanding decisions, expiry, activity/run separation, unknown outcomes, cursor gaps and failed patches. Dot tests cover absent/setup/active/paused/offline/revoked, child cancellation acknowledgement, scoped memory, export/deletion and healthy-coach silence.

Plugin tests cover all seven version axes, locality refusal, no silent cloud fallback, hash/signature/namespace rejection, undeclared imports, grant expiry/revocation, guest identity spoofing, quota exhaustion, blocking host I/O, cancellation cleanup, state migration, browser glue confinement and mobile distribution admission. Mobile tests cover safe area/keyboard/reflow, process restoration, audio routing, notification freshness and offline authorization. Browser tests cover escaped HTMX fragments, race control, sensitive history/cache handling and progressive navigation. Accessibility tests cover keyboard, screen reader, focus visibility/return, large text and reduced motion. Every pass records build/device/profile and every unsupported case remains explicit.

S19-020 · 3.2 User stories (numbered US-x; acceptance criteria in 3.3)

Governing revision: G01–16 · source requirement, not release evidence.

3.2 User stories (numbered US-x; acceptance criteria in 3.3)

  • US-1 As a user, I install a plugin from a .pxt bundle (or catalog URL) and see its features appear — navigation entries, settings sections, tools — without restarting the app.
  • US-2 As a user, I open Settings and see the plugin's settings rendered with the same components and behavior as core settings; secrets never display values.
  • US-3 As a user, I open a full plugin application (app-shell) and navigate its views; every view is native-feeling on mobile, desktop, and web.
  • US-4 As a user, I chat with an agent whose context is enriched by contributor plugins (memory, RAG, system-prompt fragments); I can inspect provenance of what was injected.
  • US-5 As a user, when the active model lacks image input, image messages are transparently routed to an installed image-inference provider plugin.
  • US-6 As a user, I trigger a workflow plugin (e.g., via a Hand) and watch its progress as live events; I can cancel it.
  • US-7 As a user, I install a service plugin; its capabilities appear as tools the agent can call, with clear trust labeling.
  • US-8 As a user, I deactivate or remove a plugin; its surfaces disappear, its sidecars stop, and (on remove) I choose whether to delete its data.
  • US-9 As a plugin author, I write a hook in Rust/TinyGo/Python/JS against the WIT, package it, and see it invoked only for the events I declared.
  • US-10 As a plugin author, unsigned bundles install only after explicit developer-mode consent, and the UI shows the trust tier.
  • US-11 As a reviewer, I can audit every lifecycle transition, policy decision, and budget overrun per plugin.
  • US-12 As a user, core features (chat, settings) behave identically before and after the plugin system ships — because they are rebuilt as plugins on the same APIs (dogfood proof).

3.3 Feature catalog with acceptance criteria

F1 — Plugin host core (knowme_plugin_host) - F1.1 Wasmtime-46 component sandbox, deny-by-default WASI, capability subset at instantiation. AC: component importing an undeclared capability fails with MissingCapability; memory/fuel limits enforced (test: fork-bomb & memory-bomb components are killed within limits). - F1.2 Manifest v2 parse/validate (parse_manifest extended). AC: invalid schema, unsupported world, or unknown capability kind → structured PluginHostError; golden-file tests per fixture. - F1.3 Signature verification (Ed25519/did:key) + CID/sha256 pinning. AC: tampered component → Invalid; unsigned → developer tier with consent record. - F1.4 Lifecycle state machine with persistence and audit. AC: crash mid-activate resumes deterministically; every transition audited. - F1.5 .cwasm precompiled cache with version-mismatch invalidation. AC: warm activation < 50 ms on desktop reference hardware.

F2 — Capability registry - F2.1 Capability cards persisted; queryable by kind, platform, trust. AC: registry survives restart; query latency < 5 ms at 500 plugins. - F2.2 Recognized set v1.0 = strategy-doc v0.1 set + app-shell, service, workflow. AC: unknown kinds rejected at manifest validation with migration note.

F3 — Hook pipeline (gen_ui_agent::pipeline) - F3.1 Typed stage enum + contribution types integrated with gen_ui_context. AC: contributions appear in assembled context with provenance tags; ordering deterministic. - F3.2 Epoch budget enforcement (default 200 ms/stage). AC: over-budget contributor dropped, knowme.plugin.budget_exceeded telemetry emitted, run continues. - F3.3 Event-subscription hooks. AC: hook fires only for declared patterns; wildcard beyond declaration rejected.

F4 — Settings substrate - F4.1 settings_definition/settings_value in SurrealDB + Postgres; scope model; secret refs. AC: schema-invalid write rejected; secret value never leaves keychain/Vault; CRDT clock merges on OFP sync. - F4.2 A2UI-generated settings forms in Flutter + React Settings screens. AC: a plugin with settings renders a section indistinguishable from core; golden tests per platform.

F5 — A2UI app-shell - F5.1 Navigation mounting of app-shell plugins on all three UI targets. AC: plugin root appears beside Chat; deep-link route works; no chrome mismatch (Flat 2.0 respected). - F5.2 Catalog merge (base + contributed, fail-closed). AC: component not in merged catalog → render error surface, never raw content. - F5.3 Action round-trip (A2uiAction → plugin on-action). AC: latency budget < 100 ms local; full integration test on mobile.

F6 — Service broker - F6.1 Port lease + supervision + health. AC: killed sidecar restarts ≤ N with backoff; deactivate frees the port (verified). - F6.2 OpenAPI ingestion → MCP tools. AC: a sample service's operations appear in tools/list within 2 s of activation; calls route through broker proxy; undeclared outbound hosts blocked. - F6.3 WASM-native service world (wasi:http-aligned). AC: same OpenAPI ingestion works for component services.

F7 — Provider plugins - F7.1 Modality registration + inference-router fallback. AC: with primary engine lacking image input and provider installed, an image message succeeds; without provider, a clear capability error surfaces. - F7.2 Streaming parity. AC: provider streams through the same InferenceEvent path as built-in engines.

F8 — Workflow plugins - F8.1 Workflow document schema + BossFang execution binding. AC: sample 3-node workflow executes on BossFang; progress emits AG-UI events; cancel propagates. - F8.2 knowme_hands::DeploymentTarget::BossFang integration. AC: a Hand referencing a workflow plugin deploys and runs end-to-end (replaces current NotImplemented).

F9 — Distribution & catalog - F9.1 IPFS/OCI fetch with pinning. AC: offline install from local bundle works; CID mismatch aborts. - F9.2 In-app plugin catalog UI (browse/install/trust badges). AC: catalog is itself an A2UI app-shell (dogfood).

F10 — Interop surfaces - F10.1 Plugin MCP server mounting. AC: plugin tools listed via gen_ui_mcp with correct trust tier and annotations. - F10.2 Plugin AgentCard + A2A reachability. AC: external A2A client can message/send to a plugin agent via the container's dispatcher. - F10.3 AG-UI emission for all plugin runs. AC: emitted events validate against uar/schemas/uar-agui-v1.schema.json (conformance test).

F11 — Migration dogfood - F11.1 Settings feature re-implemented as first-party plugin. AC: zero user-visible regression (golden UI suite). - F11.2 Chat feature consumes hook pipeline for its context assembly. AC: existing chat tests pass; provenance inspector shows core contributor.

S36-014 · Acceptance gates for the pilot

Governing revision: G01–16 · source requirement, not release evidence.

Acceptance gates for the pilot
Overclaim case
Seeded phase with a historical S4 receipt and a completion claim. Pass: coach emits one proposal naming the stale receipt; no second proposal on unchanged evidence; packet VerifiedSuccess only after a candidate-bound S4 receipt.
Budget wall case
Counters at limit, report says "2+2=4". Pass: proposal is decision_required with zero allowance granted; disposition ExhaustedAllowance, never FailedAcceptance.
Scope case
Coach discovers an attractive improvement. Pass: written to memory as retained backlog; phase closes on the adopted scope; no issue comment, no new gate.
Denied steering case
Cedar denies the coach's grant. Pass: Blocked candidate with the denial named; no retry via another path (verified by audit chain).
Healthy quiet case
Clean run. Pass: zero proposals, one terminal packet, coach cost under 2% of executor cost.
Restart case
Kill the coach mid-intervention. Pass: resumes from offset, no duplicate proposal, reconciliation record intact.

title: Decisions that remain open
text:
The recommended default is native Flutter plus shared Rust services, declarative A2UI portability, desktop/server component execution, explicit remote fallback, and LiveKit with a separate multiparty coordinator. That is sufficient to implement the first complete vertical without betting on mobile downloaded-code acceptance.

Decisions still needing implementation evidence are: the generic UAR plugin namespace/version migration; minimum production runtime/toolchain pins; mobile interpreted component admission and measured budgets; browser component adaptation; room encryption/key management and agent participation policy; recording/transcript retention; reliable delegated scheduling; and exact model/hardware presets. Marketplace revenue policy and LoRa transport remain deferred source proposals. They are not prerequisites for a working workspace.

The cost of this design is real. Shared semantics require conformance work across native and web renderers. Explicit grants add state to installation and collaboration. A multiparty voice agent needs coordination beyond a room connection. Those costs buy something concrete: the user can tell what is running, what it can see, who it represents, and whether its work actually happened.
